title: Guard Your Heart
excerpt: Above all else, guard your heart. But what if the heart can't be trusted? Proverbs, Jeremiah, and the new heart God promises.

blocks.text: If you had to pick the single most important thing to protect in your life, what would it be?

Your health? Your family? Your reputation, your savings, your faith? All reasonable answers. But the writer of Proverbs, a father giving advice to his son, picks something different. And he does it with a phrase that stops you in your tracks:

verses: Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.

blocks.text: *Above all else.* Not "among other things." Not "when you have time." Above everything, the thing to watch over is the heart. Because whatever is in there is the source, and everything else in your life, your words, your choices, your habits, your relationships, is downstream from it.
It's a great line. It's also a bit of a problem, as we'll see in a minute.
Where Do You Post the Guards?
First, notice that this verse doesn't float on its own. It sits in the middle of a short passage, and the surrounding verses read like a security plan.

Before the verse, the father talks about the *ears*: "pay attention to what I say; turn your ear to my words" (4:20). After it, he moves to the *mouth*: "Keep your mouth free of perversity; keep corrupt talk far from your lips" (4:24). Then the *eyes*: "Let your eyes look straight ahead; fix your gaze directly before you" (4:25). And finally the *feet*: "Give careful thought to the paths for your feet and be steadfast in all your ways" (4:26).

Ears, mouth, eyes, feet. They're the entry and exit points. Think of an ancient walled city. The wall doesn't matter nearly as much as the gates, because that's where everything comes in and goes out. And the father is saying: your heart is the city, and these are its gates. If you want to guard the heart, you have to watch what comes through them.
That's where this gets uncomfortably practical.
What Gets Through the Gates
Think about what you let in on an ordinary day.

Through your **eyes and ears**: hours of screens, scrolling, shows, headlines, and opinions, most of it designed to hold your attention rather than serve your good. Voices you listen to, music you play, conversations you stay in. Whatever you consistently let in, you eventually absorb. It sets your mood, shapes your assumptions, and quietly trains your desires.
Through your **mouth**: what you say shapes what you believe. Gossip, complaining, and cynical jokes may feel harmless, but repeating something long enough has a way of making it true to you.
Through your **feet**: the places you go and the paths you take. The habits that become routines, the routines that become a life.

And then there are the gates we forget about entirely, the ones on the inside. A resentment you keep rehearsing. A grudge you feed. A secret you've decided to keep. Hebrews warns about a "bitter root" that springs up and causes trouble, defiling many (12:15). Nobody plants a bitter root on purpose. It grows in the places we leave unattended.

None of this means you should wall yourself off from the world and refuse to engage. Jesus walked into messy rooms and unlikely places, and He was never contaminated by them. But He also guarded what shaped Him. He rose early to pray. He knew Scripture. He was deliberate about what He let define Him. Guarding isn't isolation. It's intention.
The Problem
Now we come to the catch I mentioned. Here is what Jeremiah says about the thing we're supposed to be guarding:

verses: The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it?

blocks.text: Wait. We're told to guard our heart above all else, and then told that heart can't be trusted? How do you guard something that lies to you?

Jesus agrees with Jeremiah, and says it with unsettling clarity: "For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, slander" (Matthew 15:19). Not the environment. Not just the world around us. The heart itself.

That's a hard thing to sit with. It means that even if you perfectly managed your inputs, deleted every app, cut off every bad influence, and filled your days with Scripture and good company, you'd still have a problem. The problem wouldn't only be what's out there. It would be what's in *here.*

This is where a lot of well-meaning advice goes wrong. If "guard your heart" were all we had, it would turn into an exhausting project of self-management, a lifetime of white-knuckled vigilance, constantly policing our thoughts and feeling like failures every time something slips through. Some people live that way, and it wears them out.
But that isn't where the Bible leaves us.
A New Heart
Here's what God says, through the prophet Ezekiel:

verses: I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.

blocks.text: Read the verbs. *I will give. I will put. I will remove.* This isn't a repair job we're expected to do ourselves. It's a transplant, and God is the surgeon. He doesn't hand us a broken heart and a to-do list. He promises to replace the heart itself, and to put His own Spirit inside to keep it alive.

This is the piece that changes everything about how we read Proverbs 4:23. We aren't guarding a heart we're trying to fix through effort. We're guarding something God has made new. It's the difference between protecting a stained, failing machine and protecting a gift. You tend it, you care for it, and you keep out what would poison it, but you do so from gratitude, not fear.
It's also why David, after his fall, didn't pray, "Help me do better." He prayed, "Create in me a clean heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10). He knew a new heart had to come from outside him.

And there's one more thing, tucked in the New Testament, that I find deeply comforting. Paul writes: "the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7).

Look at who's doing the guarding there. It's God's peace. *He* stands at the gate. We're not carrying this alone. Our job is to keep showing up, to keep bringing our anxieties to Him in prayer, as the verses before it describe, and to let His peace do what our own vigilance never could.
So What Does Guarding Actually Look Like?
If it isn't grim self-policing, then what is it? A few things come to mind.

**Pay attention to what you're feeding on.** Notice what leaves you drained, anxious, bitter, or numb, and what leaves you steadier. You don't need a rigid system. Just start by noticing, and then make one small change.

**Fill the space with something better.** It's hard to simply remove bad input; it works better to replace it. "Whatever is true, whatever is noble, whatever is right, whatever is pure... think about such things" (Philippians 4:8). The psalmist says, "I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you" (Psalm 119:11). A heart stocked with Scripture has less room for the junk.

**Invite God to search what you can't see.** Since we can't fully understand our own hearts, we ask the One who can. "Search me, God, and know my heart... See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting" (Psalm 139:23–24). It's a brave prayer. It's also a safe one, because the One searching is the One who loves you.
**Deal with the small things early.** Bitterness, secret habits, quiet compromises. Address them while they're small, with God and with a trusted friend. Roots are easier to pull when they're young.

**Give yourself grace.** You will still fail at this. Something will get through the gate. When it does, you don't need to panic or spiral. You go to the One who promised to make you new, and you start again.
The Source Matters
Everything you do flows from it. Your words, your patience, your love, your choices, even the way you handle a hard Tuesday. That's what makes the heart worth guarding above all else.

But the good news of the gospel is that you were never meant to guard it by yourself, or to fix it by yourself. You have a new heart on the way, and a God who stands at the gate. So guard it, not from fear but from love, and let Him keep making it more like His own.

items: What are you letting through the "gates" most often? Think about what you watch, listen to, say, and dwell on. What is one input you could reduce or replace this week to protect your heart?
Is there a "bitter root" or hidden resentment you've been leaving unattended? What would it look like to bring it to God, or to a trusted friend, before it grows?
Do you tend to guard your heart out of fear or out of trust? How does knowing that God promises a new heart, and stands guard through His peace, change the way you approach it?

blocks.text: Lord, thank You that You don't ask me to fix my own heart. Forgive me for the things I've let in, and for the places I've guarded poorly. Search me, and show me what I can't see. Give me the new heart You promised, and let Your peace stand guard over my heart and mind. Help me protect what You've made new, not out of fear, but because I love You. Amen.
